title: The IB Goes Digital: What November 2026's Online Exam Shift Means for Teachers
excerpt: IB digital exams arrive for all schools in November 2026, alongside redesigned History and Global Politics guides. Here's what actually changes in your classroom.
content:
The IB Goes Digital: What November 2026's Online Exam Shift Means for Teachers

If you've taught the IB for more than a few years, you've already lived through one syllabus rewrite that made your carefully built assessment folder obsolete overnight. This one is bigger. Starting in November 2026, every IB World School gets the option to sit Language and Literature and Language Acquisition exams on screen instead of on paper. The pilot phase is over. What's starting now is a multi-year transition that will eventually touch every subject you teach.

That's the headline. The part that actually affects your Monday-to-Friday teaching is what's happening underneath it: several Diploma Programme subject guides have been rewritten from the ground up, with new assessment structures, new internal assessment formats, and new expectations for how you plan a unit. If you teach History, Global Politics, Mathematics, or Computer Science, some of this has already landed on your desk. If it hasn't yet, it will.

What's actually changing in November

The IB's Digital Examination System launched in January 2026, and sample digital papers went out to schools the year before that, in May 2025 [1]. A select group of schools ran the first live digital exams in May 2026. Come November, that option opens to every IB World School for two subjects: Language and Literature and Language Acquisition [1].

Here's the part worth knowing before a student or a parent asks you about it. During this rollout, students choose between the digital and paper version of the exam, and the paper itself is identical either way. Grade boundaries are set so a student gets the same result regardless of which format they sit [1]. Matt Glanville, the IB's Director of Assessment, has framed the push less as a cost-cutting move and more as an accessibility one: digital exams "massively increase the range of accessibility functions" for students and let them "take control of their own engagement with the assessment" [1].

More subjects follow between 2026 and 2029, starting with Individuals and Societies, Sciences, and Mathematics, and the IB expects every exam to run digitally by the early 2030s [1]. That's a long runway, but the November 2026 rollout is the moment it stops being theoretical.

The syllabus rewrites are the part that changes your actual teaching

Digital delivery is one shift. The other, quieter one is that several DP subjects have entirely new guides, and they change what and how you assess, not just what device a student uses.

History got a full redesign for first teaching in August 2026, with first assessment in May 2028 [2]. The old prescribed-subjects model is gone. Teachers now build courses around Paired Case Studies for Paper 1, a Global Theme the school selects for Paper 2, and, at Higher Level, a Regional In-Depth Topic drawn from one of four world regions [2]. The Internal Assessment drops its old reflection section and moves to three parts: Inquiry Question, Sources and Perspectives, and Synthesis and Evaluation [2]. If you've taught the same case studies for a decade, you're choosing new ones this year.

Global Politics is already mid-transition. The revised guide launched for first teaching in August 2024, with the new assessment structure first examined in May 2026, so this year's cohort is the first to sit it [3]. The subject dropped from sixteen core concepts to four (power, sovereignty, legitimacy, interdependence), the old Levels of Analysis section is now called Scale, and the Higher Level Presentations disappeared entirely in favor of a new Paper 3 built around eight Global Political Challenges, up from six under the old guide [4][3]. The internal assessment was renamed from Engagement Activity to Political Engagement Project, and the hours and word counts are now specified: 25 hours and a 2,000 to 2,400 word report at Standard Level, 35 hours plus an extra 400 words for a recommendation section at Higher Level [4].

Mathematics (both Analysis and Approaches, and Applications and Interpretation) and Computer Science are on a first-assessment-2027 timeline, with updated resource volumes already appearing from IB-aligned publishers [5]. If you teach either subject, next year's planning cycle is when the changes reach your classroom.

What this actually means for your week

None of this is optional reading. A few practical consequences worth naming plainly:

Your assessment bank needs rebuilding, not tweaking. New paper structures and new command terms mean old past papers stop being reliable practice material. History teachers, in particular, are choosing entirely new case studies and themes this year, not adapting existing ones [2].

IA supervision changes with the format as much as the content. Simplified sections sound like less work, but they also mean less room for students to recover a weak submission through a reflection component that no longer exists. You'll need to front-load the planning stages harder than before.

Digital exam familiarity is now a teaching-practice question, not just an IT one. Even if your subject isn't in the November 2026 rollout, students in your school will be sitting digital papers in other classes. Building even light on-screen practice into your own formative assessments now saves a scramble later.

Getting ahead of it through professional development

The IB structures its workshops in three tiers. Category 1 is an entry-level introduction to programme structure, Category 2 goes deeper into curriculum design and pedagogy, and Category 3 is aimed specifically at subject expertise and guide updates like the ones described above [6]. Schools going through an evaluation period are required to have at least one teacher per subject group complete a Category 3 workshop, and every new hire in that window needs at least a Category 1, 2, or 3 session under their belt [6].

In-person workshops typically run about two and a half days; online versions stretch over roughly four weeks of self-paced work [6]. Third-party providers run sessions too. CASIE, for example, has Global Politics and History-adjacent Category 3 offerings scheduled for October and November 2026, priced separately for virtual and in-person attendance [6]. If your subject guide changed and you haven't booked a Category 3 workshop yet, that's the single most useful hour you can spend this term.

Key Takeaways

  • Digital exams open to all IB World Schools for Language and Literature and Language Acquisition in November 2026, following a limited-school pilot in May 2026 [1].
  • Students choose paper or digital format during the rollout; the exam content and grade boundaries stay the same either way [1].
  • History has a full curriculum redesign for first teaching August 2026 (first assessment May 2028), built around Paired Case Studies, a Global Theme, and Regional In-Depth Topics at HL [2].
  • Global Politics is now first-assessed under its new guide as of May 2026: four core concepts instead of sixteen, a new Paper 3, and a renamed, hour-specified Political Engagement Project [3][4].
  • Category 3 IB workshops are the standard route to prepare for a subject-guide change, and schools under evaluation must have at least one teacher per subject group complete one [6].

Don't wait for your department meeting to figure out which of these changes lands on your subject and when. Check your subject's first-assessment date against the IB's own curriculum updates page, and book a Category 3 workshop before the term you're expected to teach the new guide starts.
